newsitem.title: UK: Clyde, Gulf Canada lock horns again.
newsitem.headline: Clyde, Gulf Canada lock horns again.

text.p: Britain's Clyde Petroleum named its price on Tuesday, producing figures to try to prove that a hostile 432 million pound ($696.9 million) bid by Gulf Canada Resources was too low.
It convinced analysts -- but not its predator.

On the last day in which the oil exploration and production company was allowed to release new financial information, Clyde said an independent consultancy had valued its net assets at 120 to 144 pence per share compared to Gulf Canada's 105p bid.
"Most people who are not associated with Gulf believe its bid undervalues Clyde's assets and future," said analyst Jurjen Lunshof at Credit Lyonnais Laing.
It was the first time Clyde pointed at its net asset value to fight off Gulf Canada.
Market estimates on Clyde's net assets had ranged roughly between 70 and 80 pence per share.
Chairman Malcolm Gourlay said in a statement: "Now it is crystal clear quite how seriously Gulf Canada has undervalued Clyde's potential under its existing management team."
Clyde also announced a 21.7 percent increase in full-year earnings and forecast that its operating cash flow would grow by 18 percent to at least 150 million pounds in 1997.
While the company's shares ended 1.5 pence lower at 117 pence, it stated that independent cash flow studies also implied the stock should be trading at at least 144 pence.

"Whether you use cash flow multiples or net asset values, Gulf Canada's offer comes nowhere near the value of Clyde's existing business let alone its future potential," said managing director Roy Franklin.

Gulf Canada, however, said Clyde's defence was based on unrealistic assumptions on oil price, discount rate and exchange rate. It pointed to petroleum consultancy Scientific Software-Intercomp, which says that the Clyde camp understates the technical risks of future projects.
"The valuation put forward by Clyde's board is not credible," said Gulf Canada's president and chief executive officer J.P. Bryan.
Gulf Canada Resources launched its hostile bid for Clyde on December 18. On Monday, it extended the bid to February 4 after receiving acceptances for a mere 0.17 percent of Clyde's shares.
Shares in Clyde, which have consistently hovered well above Gulf Canada's offer, still reflect market hopes of a higher bid emerging, analysts said.

Meanwhile, Clyde said it expected production to rise by nine percent to an average 44,900 barrels of oil equivalent per day (boepd) and increase further to an average 55,200 boepd in 1998 and 60,200 in 1999.
Earnings rose to 32.0 million pounds in 1996 from 26.3 million pound the previous year thanks to increased production and higher oil and gas prices.
Clyde, which is mainly active in the North Sea, Australia and Indonesia, said it was looking for new venture opportunities in Australia after acquiring Crusader Ltd last year.

"Clyde's strategy is to increase production and reserves in order to sustain earnings and cash flow growth, through a balanced programme of acquisition, development and exploration," it said. ($1=.6199 Pound)
